description: The command line's contract, as data. Every implementation runs this file and must agree — exit code first, then what reached stdout and stderr. Derived from typescript/test/cli/*.test.ts, which was the only place the behaviour was written down when the first ports were built; there are five implementations now, and this file is the only thing holding their command lines together.

schema.name: what the case is for, used in the test report
schema.command: which entry point: 'main' (default), 'init' or 'pack'. init and pack take the temp directory as their working directory, which is why they are named rather than passed as argv.
schema.files: relative path -> contents, written into a fresh temp directory before the run
schema.registry: true to build the standard demo registry in the temp directory and make {registry} available
schema.argv: arguments. {dir} becomes the temp directory's absolute path, {registry} its registry URL
schema.stdout: exact stdout, when the output is the point
schema.stdoutMatches: a regular expression stdout must match
schema.stderrContains: substrings that must appear on stderr
schema.wrote: relative path -> exact contents the run must have left behind
schema.wroteContains: relative path -> substrings the file must contain
schema.only: implementations this case runs in. Absent means all five. Present means the others do not support the feature yet — the case stays here, named and visible, rather than being deleted and forgotten.
schema.note: why the case is shaped the way it is, when that is not obvious

cases.name: --help exits 0 and prints usage
-h exits 0 and prints usage
--help describes --now in the same words everywhere
stdoutContains: --now <date>             Pin the clock date generators read as "now" —
cases.note: The five help texts already differ on --jobs, each describing its own threading. The clock does not vary by implementation, so its wording should not either — and the wrapping is pinned because that is the part that drifts when somebody edits one file.

cases.name: --version prints the declared version
cases.note: The exact number, not a shape. A shape is what let two implementations ship a hardcoded 0.1.0 while the fixture stayed green. Bump this with the version in all five build files.

cases.name: -v prints the declared version
cases.note: The exact number, not a shape. A shape is what let two implementations ship a hardcoded 0.1.0 while the fixture stayed green. Bump this with the version in all five build files.

cases.name: no input exits 2 and points at --help
an unknown option exits 2
a missing option value exits 2 and names the option
an invalid --count exits 2 before anything is rendered
a second positional argument exits 2
an invalid --engine exits 2 and lists the engines
a --now the date generator cannot read exits 2
cases.note: Refused, never quietly replaced by the real clock — a silent fallback would hand back the very irreproducibility the flag exists to remove.

cases.name: a --now carrying a zone suffix exits 2
cases.note: The flag takes exactly what <gen type="date" value="…"> takes, and that syntax carries no zone: every date in the engine is UTC. Accepting a Z here would be a second date syntax for the same project.

cases.name: a missing --now value exits 2 and names the option

generated records go to stdout by default
-o writes to the named file and nothing to stdout
--output is the long spelling of -o
long options are accepted in --name=value form
--count overrides the count in <env>
--now is the date every generator reading "today" sees
cases.note: Without the flag this case could only assert a shape, because the answer changes at midnight. The wall clock was the fifth input to a run and the only one the command line could not name.

cases.name: --now accepts a time, in the date generator's own syntax
--now makes person.b_day reproduce byte for byte
cases.note: b_day is a window measured back from now, so these three dates move a day per day without the flag. They are the reason it exists.

cases.name: init honours --locale

pack --help prints usage and exits 0
cases.note: Runs before the pack store is resolved, so it works on a machine where init has never run — which is where somebody needs it.

cases.name: pack -h prints usage and exits 0
pack without a config says to run init first
pack list names the bundle and its description
pack add unpacks the address path straight into the store
cases.note: The archive nests its files under `demo/packs/`, which is the bundler's business: both levels are stripped so what lands in the store is the address path and nothing else. One store, one dataPaths entry, however many bundles go in.

cases.name: pack add writes down what the bundle owns
cases.note: With every bundle in one tree, a folder named after the bundle no longer exists, so the store keeps books: the paths each bundle owns (the shallowest folder holding all its files — here `demo/person`, since the demo bundle is one file), its version, its digest. `remove` deletes exactly those paths and `list` marks installed from this file. It is a DOTFILE because the store is a scan root and the loader skips ignored names, not unknown extensions — `installed.json` here would load as a pack at address `installed`. The sha256 is not pinned: each runner builds its own archive and only the extracted contents have to agree.

cases.name: format refuses a file it cannot parse and leaves it untouched
format with no file is a usage error
a project config's locale does not override what the config declares
cases.note: local="zz" names a locale nobody ships, so the run must FAIL. If a project config's locale="en" wrongly overrode it, the address would resolve under `en` and the run would succeed with English surnames — which is what TypeScript did before the fix. Only the exit code is asserted: the three disagree about whether an unknown-locale address is a validator diagnostic (TDC071) or a render-time error, and that is a separate question from the one this case exists to pin.

cases.name: pack list prints the catalogue in the shared shape
cases.stdout:
Available data packs:

  demo                      Demo pack (0.0 MB)
               two surnames

Install with: tdcv2 pack add <id>

cases.name: pack list marks what is already installed
cases.stdout:
Available data packs:

  demo         ✓ installed  Demo pack (0.0 MB)
               two surnames

Install with: tdcv2 pack add <id>
cases.note: The mark comes from the store's books, not from a folder with the bundle's name — there are no such folders any more. A tree somebody unpacked by hand is therefore not "installed": nothing records what it owns, so nothing could remove it cleanly either.

cases.name: pack add reports each bundle, its file count and where it was registered
registering a pack keeps every other key the config already had
pack remove deletes the tree the record names, and nothing beside it
cases.note: No network: removal reads the store's books. `countries/atlantis` goes and the now-empty `countries/` goes with it, while the bundle sharing the tree is untouched — which is the whole reason the paths are recorded rather than guessed from the id. The store stays in `dataPaths` because something is still in it; it is unregistered only when the last bundle leaves.

cases.name: a store in the old per-bundle layout is moved to the flat one
cases.stdout:
Available data packs:

  demo         ✓ installed  Demo pack (0.0 MB)
               two surnames

Install with: tdcv2 pack add <id>
cases.note: Everyone who ran `pack add` before the flat store has `<store>/<id>/packs/…` on disk and one dataPaths entry per bundle, and neither `list` nor `remove` can read that any more. So the FIRST `tdcv2 pack` of any kind moves it, in place, and says what it did — on stderr, because the catalogue on stdout is something people pipe. Version and sha256 are empty: the archive is long gone and nothing here is going to invent them. It happens once; a store already flat is left alone. `pack --help` runs before this, so it still works on a machine where nothing is set up.

cases.name: a bundle whose bytes do not match the index is refused before it is unpacked
the project config is found from the .tdc file, not from the shell's directory
cases.note: Every runner invokes the CLI in-process, so the working directory is the checkout and not {dir}. Searching for tdcv2.config.json from there would miss this one and fall back to the bundled English — a run that succeeds with the wrong data. The pack a project installed belongs to the config file that sits beside it.

cases.name: the project config's locale fills in when the config declares none
cases.note: `init` asks for a locale and writes it down, so a project that answered `ru` should not have to repeat local="ru" in every .tdc. It is a DEFAULT and never an override — the case above pins the other half, that a config declaring its own locale keeps it. Both files sit in a dataPath, so this reads the fixture's own two words and never a bundled pack, whichever ones an implementation happens to ship.

cases.name: a pack file is placed by its header, not by its path
cases.note: Two routes, one file each: `address:` names the address outright, and `locale:` supplies the missing locale for a path-derived one. Both let someone keep a flat folder of their own lists instead of rebuilding the locale tree to hold two files, and both have to work in every implementation — the reference builds an address index when it scans, and the ports build the same index the first time a path lookup misses.

cases.name: a pack file that lands at no address is named, not merely missed
cases.note: The file carries a header, so it was meant as a pack, but `stray` names no locale, country or `common` and nothing in the header says where it belongs — so it is dropped, and the address it was asked for cannot resolve. Both halves have to be said: TDC071 alone sends the author to the config, which is right, while the file that was silently discarded sits in the folder next to it. cases.name: a run too big for this machine's memory is refused before it starts
cases.note: Two billion records held in RAM is hundreds of gigabytes on any reading of the estimate, so the answer does not depend on the machine running the test — which is what lets this be a shared case at all. The numbers in the message legitimately differ (a JVM reports its heap ceiling, the others the physical total, and a run to stdout is charged for the string it builds while `-o` is not); the code, the refusal and the silent stdout do not. `mode="memory"` is what makes count a memory cost: the streaming engines hold one row.
stderrContains: run will likely thrash or crash

cases.name: a refusal the streaming engine words itself reaches the user unprefixed
cases.note: A running total is the accumulation of every row before it, so it is refused by name rather than approximated — and the sentence saying so is written at the refusal, complete. Every port used to add its exception class's own prefix on top ("stream mode: ", and Rust "not ported yet: ", which additionally called a deliberate design limit unfinished work), so one refusal read four ways depending on which package was installed. Pinned WITH the leading "tdcv2: " precisely so a second prefix breaks this case.

gaps.pack header warnings for a file nothing: TDC171 itself is no longer a gap — all five name the dropped file, and the case above pins it. What differs is WHEN. The reference reads every pack root before it starts, so it warns about an unplaceable file even when no config mentions it; the ports build that index only once a lookup has missed, which is the moment the author is looking for the file anyway. Measured, the reference's scan is 4100 files and ~240 ms per process against a bundled set that has never produced a single warning, so the ports keep the lazy scan on purpose. The one case it cannot reach: a stray file sitting beside packs a config uses successfully stays unreported outside TypeScript.
gaps.TDC160, TDC161 and TDC162: Three render-time refusals about an INLINE <gen> — `row=` on one, weighted advanced_regex choices, a non-numeric counter start or step. No implementation can reach them from its command line, the reference included: a <gen> inside <line> is TDC131/TDC132 and one directly inside <block> is TDC013, all raised by the validator before anything renders, and the TDC facade validates too. They are reachable only through TypeScript's low-level render(parse(src).tree) entry point, which walks an unvalidated AST — a shape the ports do not have, because they compile a config into a model rather than rendering the tree. Porting them would mean first accepting a config all five currently refuse.

registryBundle.note: The zip nests everything under `<id>/packs/`. That nesting is the bundler's, not the store's: `pack add` strips both levels while extracting, so this archive lands at <store>/demo/person/lastName.txt. An entry that does not carry the `<id>/packs/` prefix means the archive is not the bundle it claims to be, and the whole thing is refused rather than scattered into a shared tree. Every runner builds exactly this, because the layout is the registry's and getting it wrong breaks packs published for the other implementations.
